title: A Beginner's Guide to Interval and Speed Workouts
seo_title: A Beginner's Guide to Interval and Speed Workouts
meta_description: What interval training actually is, why it's added to a base of easy running rather than replacing it, and two simple workouts to start with.
dek: Interval training is where a lot of runners first feel real progress -- and where a lot of runners first get hurt or burned out by doing too much, too soon.

sections.heading: What Interval Training Actually Is
paragraphs: Interval training is structured, repeated hard effort broken up by periods of recovery -- a set of faster reps run at a controlled pace, separated by easy jogging or standing rest, rather than one continuous hard effort from start to finish. The recovery between reps is what makes the workout work: it lets a runner accumulate more total time at a challenging pace than a single unbroken hard effort would allow, because the body gets brief chances to partially recover before the next rep starts.

This is different from a tempo run, which is a single sustained effort at a hard-but-manageable pace, and different from a long run, which is about time on feet rather than speed. Intervals are specifically about teaching the body to run faster than usual, in short, repeatable doses -- building the top-end speed and running economy that easy running alone doesn't develop.

sections.heading: Why Intervals Sit on Top of an Easy-Running Base
paragraphs: Intervals are an addition to a training week, not a substitute for the easy running that should still make up most of it. The physiological case for mostly-easy running -- covered in this site's guide to easy pace -- doesn't stop applying once a runner starts adding speed work; it's the reason speed work is added on top of an aerobic base rather than instead of one. A runner with a thin base of easy mileage who jumps straight into hard interval sessions is building speed on a foundation that isn't ready to support it.

In practice this means a beginner shouldn't add intervals until easy running feels genuinely comfortable and sustainable across several weeks, and even then, intervals should typically make up a small fraction of total weekly running -- one focused session a week is usually enough for a beginner, with the rest of the week staying easy.

sections.heading: Two Simple Beginner Workout Structures
paragraphs: A straightforward starting structure is short, repeated efforts with equal recovery: six repetitions of two minutes at a pace that feels comfortably hard -- not an all-out sprint -- followed by two minutes of easy jogging or walking between each. The even recovery keeps the pace honest and prevents the first rep from being run far harder than the last, which is a common early mistake.

A gentler entry point is an unstructured fartlek: after an easy warm-up, alternate roughly one minute at a faster, purposeful effort with two to three minutes back at easy pace, repeated for fifteen to twenty minutes, judged entirely by feel rather than a stopwatch. Because there's no fixed pace target, a fartlek session is a low-pressure way to get used to shifting gears mid-run before moving to more structured, watch-driven interval sessions.

sections.heading: Common Beginner Mistakes
paragraphs: The most common mistake is treating the first rep of an interval session like a personal-best attempt -- starting far faster than the pace can be sustained for the remaining reps, then fading badly by the third or fourth. A well-run interval session holds a roughly even, controlled pace across every rep; if the first rep feels easy, that's usually a sign the pace is about right, not a sign to go faster.

The second common mistake is letting interval sessions crowd out the easy-running base that's supposed to support them -- adding a second or third hard session because progress from the first one felt good, or cutting the easy days short to fit more speed work in. Extra hard sessions add fatigue faster than most beginners can recover from, and the base they're built on erodes exactly when it's needed most.

faqs.question: How many interval sessions should a beginner do per week?
faqs.answer: One focused interval session a week is usually enough for a beginner, with the rest of the week spent on easy running. Adding more hard sessions before a solid easy-running base is established tends to increase injury and burnout risk faster than it increases fitness.

faqs.question: How fast should interval reps be run?
faqs.answer: Comfortably hard, not all-out -- a pace that's clearly faster than easy running but sustainable across every rep in the set. If the pace fades noticeably by the final rep, the earlier reps were likely run too fast for the workout to hold together.

faqs.question: Do I need a track or GPS watch to do interval training?
faqs.answer: No -- an unstructured fartlek, alternating faster and easy effort by feel over a set total time, is a beginner-friendly way to start without any equipment. A track or watch becomes more useful later for holding consistent, even paces across structured reps.
